stories.headline: Update: Zelensky Says US Floated Ukraine Ceding Donbas in Exchange for NATO Membership
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday that US negotiators had raised the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership. "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," he told reporters. He said the proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda."

The comments followed visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to Moscow, where they met President Vladimir Putin, and to an EU summit in Dublin, where they met Zelensky on Thursday. US officials had previously said Ukrainian NATO membership was off the table, and Russia has said another NATO member on its border is unacceptable. Zelensky said that if he received a proposal containing security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds for reconstruction, he would put it to a referendum.

Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of Donetsk and Luhansk, which make up the Donbas. Ceding the small portions Ukraine still holds would be symbolically significant, since it would amount to accepting the region as Russian. Kyiv has consistently said it will not give up sovereign territory, while Moscow has demanded it do so, along with limits on Ukraine's military and guaranteed neutrality.

Zelensky cautioned that Putin's signals suggested "an extremely difficult conversation," and comments by Kremlin officials indicate Russia's position has not shifted. Relations between Kyiv and Washington have also been strained over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities, which President Trump had asked Ukraine to pause.

stories.headline: Hungarian Authorities Uncover $20 Million in Cash in Probe of Former Orbán Minister
stories.summary:
Hungarian authorities said nearly $20 million in cash was found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into Miklós Seszták, a former minister of national development under Viktor Orbán. Seszták is accused of accepting bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company, and he denies wrongdoing. The search lasted two days across secluded locations around the country.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office said investigators found banknotes in safes, woodlands, and agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses. The total was 5,071,632,000 forints, 2,658,350 euros and $1,257,100, worth about $19.5 million combined. The money has been deposited in the Hungarian State Treasury.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who unseated Orbán in a landslide election in April on a promise of sweeping anti-corruption action, described the find as the end of the "mafia." The office was created to investigate alleged graft under Orbán, a drive Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory." Seszták, another former minister and ex-central bank chief Gyorgy Matolcsy have been under arrest since September in separate graft investigations; all deny wrongdoing.

On Monday, authorities also detained Orbán's brother and three others in a people-smuggling case. Orbán dismissed the action as political revenge, saying the aim was "the elimination of the political opponent and the establishment of a one-party system." He has long denied accusations of cronyism during his 16 years in power.

stories.headline: Alaska Voters Reject Repeal of Ranked Choice Voting and Top-Four Primaries
stories.summary:
Alaskans have decided to keep ranked choice voting, rejecting a ballot measure that sought to repeal the system, according to a projection by NBC News. It is the second time voters have turned down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which they first approved in 2020.

A previous repeal attempt in 2024 also failed, narrowly. The system includes a nonpartisan top-four primary followed by ranked choice voting in the general election.

The result keeps in place the framework under which this year's high-profile Alaska contests, including the still-close Senate race, were decided.

stories.headline: Bomb Found Near Peoria, Illinois, Ethanol Plant Prompts Mile-Wide Evacuation
stories.summary:
A bomb found near an industrial building in Peoria, Illinois, forced all residents within a one-mile radius to evacuate. Police said a suspicious package was found near the BioUrja ethanol plant at about 2 p.m. Friday, and hours later it was determined to be a credible threat. The package was rendered safe at 9:12 p.m.

Police Chief Brad Dixon said the wider facility had not been declared safe and that an exhaustive search for other possible devices would continue. Mayor Rita Ali noted the plant holds ethanol and highly combustible chemicals. The FBI has deployed personnel alongside local, county and state agencies.

FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley said investigators would work to identify the person responsible. Gov. JB Pritzker said he was monitoring the situation and had directed Illinois State Police to coordinate with local authorities. Residents needing shelter were directed to Manual Academy, and a Jon Pardi concert in the area was canceled.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Agrees to Hear Challenge to Trump's Suspension of Asylum Access at Southern Border
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide the legality of President Donald Trump's executive order suspending access to the asylum system and other legal protections for migrants who cross the southern border illegally. The administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court decisions that found it was unlawful to block asylum applications under an order that described the situation at the border as an "invasion."

The administration has credited the policy with helping reduce border crossings, and argues the president has the authority to restrict asylum claims in response to what it calls an emergency. Immigrant advocates and the lower courts that ruled against the order have held that federal immigration law guarantees migrants the right to seek asylum regardless of how they enter the country, and that the president cannot override that statutory right by proclamation.

The case gives the court a chance to rule on the limits of executive power over immigration, one of the central domestic policy fights of the Trump administration. Arguments are expected to be scheduled in the coming months, with a decision likely by the end of the court's term. The outcome could shape border enforcement policy for this and future administrations.

stories.headline: Update: Democrat Eileen Laubacher Defeats Rep. Lauren Boebert; Kreiss-Tomkins Wins Alaska Governor's Race
stories.summary:
Democrat Eileen Laubacher defeated Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado's congressional race, ousting the three-term Republican and prominent ally of President Trump, NBC News and other outlets projected. Boebert had been running in a more conservative district after a close re-election in 2022, but this year's Democratic wave swept her out of office.

Separately, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins was projected to win the Alaska governor's race under ranked-choice voting, defeating Republican Bernadette Wilson, who was endorsed by Trump. He becomes the first Democrat elected to the office in more than 20 years, and at 37 will be the state's youngest governor. His victory means Democrats will hold governorships in 30 states. Democrat Cindy Holscher also narrowly won the Kansas governor's race over Republican Ty Masterson.

The results add to a broad Democratic midterm performance that gives the party control of the House and Senate in the new year. Republicans are assessing the losses, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying "politics requires more than simply winning elections," while Democrats say they have a mandate to deliver on costs. Twenty-four races in Alaska, including the Senate contest between Sen. Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola, remain uncalled.

stories.headline: Trump to Meet Xi and Putin in First-Ever Trilateral Summit at APEC in China
stories.summary:
The White House said President Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on November 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. It will be the first-ever trilateral meeting of the leaders of the world's three biggest nuclear powers.

A White House spokeswoman said Trump plans to discuss the "reduction of nuclear weapons" and the Iran war, which entered its ninth month. A senior administration official said Trump is not expected to raise Russia's war in Ukraine, and will not discuss with Xi the scandal surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy. Trump will also attend the ASEAN summit in the Philippines on the Asia trip.

The meeting comes as US envoys have held talks with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine, and as the Kremlin renews demands for a new European security architecture. Critics of the format are likely to question whether Europe and Ukraine are being sidelined, while supporters of the approach see direct engagement among the major powers as a route to arms control and an end to regional conflicts.

stories.headline: Trump Administration Delays Medicaid Work Requirements by Six Months
stories.summary:
The Trump administration announced Friday a six-month delay in enforcing Medicaid work requirements that were scheduled to take effect January 1. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said states may use an optional "hold harmless" transition period through June 30.

The requirements, established by Republicans in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, will technically still take effect on January 1. State officials had warned they were not ready to administer the rules, which require many able-bodied adults to work, volunteer or attend school to keep coverage. Estimates have suggested millions of people could lose health insurance under the policy.

Supporters of the requirements say they encourage work and protect the program's resources, while critics argue they create administrative hurdles that strip coverage from eligible people. The delay gives states additional time to build systems, and comes after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections, setting up further debate over the policy in the new year.
